lines.note: Tanomizucunai describes something offering little hope. The entry's example on the following lines applies the same lack of confidence to a person.
The example Tanomizucunai fito describes a person in whom little confidence can be placed. The Portuguese relative clause continues on the next line.
This completes the description of an unreliable person. It closes the example under Tanomizucunai rather than introducing another headword.
Tanomo is equated with Ta, fields or flooded agricultural ground. The terminal roman P. marks poetic usage and is separate from the italic Portuguese definition.

runs.text: Couſa em que ſe tem eſperança, ou

lines.note: Tanomoxij concerns something in which one has hope. The alternative phrasing, having confidence, continues on the next physical line.
The second formulation describes having confidence and completes the main definition. The following indented forms are derivatives within the same entry.
Tanomoxiſa is the related nominal form, printed alone without a separate Portuguese definition. Its indentation and roman type connect it to Tanomoxij.
Tanomoxǔ is marked as an adverb. The pilcrow introduces an example beginning with the same form; its verb and explanation follow on the next line.
Vomô completes the example Tanomoxǔ vomô, to have hopes or trust. This line closes the adverbial example under Tanomoxij.
Tanomu is illustrated by Tanomuno tçuitachi. The Portuguese translation begins the first day, divided Pri- / meiro across physical lines.
The expression denotes the first day of the eighth lunar month. The nasal mark in lũa and the historical calendrical wording are retained.
Tanôna is a cross-reference to Tanô, the earlier entry about many accomplishments. Its circumflex and the printed punctuation after Vide are preserved.
Here Tanoxij is illustrated by a wealthy or well-provided person. This historical material-abundance sense is not flattened into the modern association with enjoyment.
The opening fragment completes abaſtado. A new example, Tanoxij coto, introduces abundance, with an additional Portuguese equivalent on the following line.
The example concerns a prosperous household. Qenai fucqi xite is the incorporated reading; the u in fucqi and portions of xite are abraded, so the nonblocking uncertainty is recorded.
Coto completes the divided Japanese example, followed by the roman citation label Feiq. The Portuguese reference and translation are italic; Acaſa retains its joined source spacing.

runs.text: tãdo rica, & abastada, a abũdancia era immẽſa.

lines.note: The translation says that, with the household rich and well supplied, its abundance was immense. The printed nasal abbreviations and spelling immẽſa are retained.
Tanoximi is defined as contentment and pleasures. This noun entry is separate from the following verbal headword, even though their printed stems coincide.
The first example describes pleasures coming to an end. The Portuguese infinitive construction continues below and belongs to the noun entry Tanoximi.
Os gostos completes the ending-of-pleasures explanation. A contrasting example, Tanoximini ſacayuru, introduces flourishing in enjoyment and prosperity.
This translates the preceding example as being in great delights and prosperity. It closes the examples under the noun Tanoximi.
The verbal Tanoximi gives its inflected forms and means to enjoy oneself or indulge in pleasures. Its final complement continues on the next line.
Gostos completes the expression for giving oneself to pleasures. This short indented continuation closes the verbal Tanoximi entry.
This compound verb means to flourish in prosperity and good living. The nasal abbreviation cõ and the division proſ- are retained.
The line completes prosperidades and adds a good life. It closes the compound Tanoximi ſacaye entry without introducing another Japanese form.
This Tanpan concerns coarse or poorly prepared food, with Japanese glosses Arai-i and Soſǒna mexi. Their visibly italic initials are retained rather than silently regularized.
The Portuguese completes the coarse-food definition. Vt introduces Tanpannimo, an example whose Japanese predicate continues on the next line.
The example says that even poor food will satisfy hunger. Vyeuo is the hunger object; the Portuguese concessive translation continues below.
The translation concludes that the speaker will satisfy hunger even with bad, coarse food. It closes the first Tanpan entry.

runs.text: Hũa mezinha de cor verde como azi-

lines.note: This distinct Tanpan names a medicinal substance of a green colour compared with verdigris. The comparison word is divided azi- / nhaure across lines.
The fragment completes azinhaure, the historical verdigris comparison. This is part of the source's medicinal description, not a present-day treatment recommendation.
Tanpat is glossed by Mijicaqi camigue, short hair. The Portuguese specifies the hair's location in the indented continuation below.
Da cabeça specifies hair of the head. This continuation closes the short-hair definition under Tanpat and does not begin a separate entry.

runs.text: Catana, ou outra arma ſe melhãte. ¶

lines.note: Tãpei denotes a sword or comparable weapon. The abraded p is supported by the repeated form in the example; the visible spacing in ſe melhãte is retained.
Pei completes Tanpei in an example of fighting with this weapon. Its fuller explanation on the next lines describes close and potentially fatal combat.

runs.text: i, vir a mãos de maneira cõoutro, q̃ ou ambos

lines.note: The explanation means coming to blows with another person in such a way that either both die or one kills the other. The close-set cõoutro remains as printed.

runs.text: morrão, ou hũ mate a outro.

lines.note: This completes the description of combat ending in both opponents' deaths or one killing the other. The nasal forms are retained as source orthography.

runs.text: Hũ vaſo em que metem agoa quente

lines.note: Tanpo is a vessel filled with hot water. The following physical line explains its use as a bed warmer rather than an ordinary drinking container.

runs.text: peraſe quentar pondo o apardeſi na cama.

lines.note: The vessel is placed beside oneself in bed for warmth. The joined source forms peraſe and apardeſi are preserved instead of respaced into modern Portuguese.
Tanpopo is described simply as an herb bearing that name. The mixed long and short s in aſsi is retained; no botanical identification is added to the canonical text.
Tanpu is illustrated by Tanpuni canǒ, followed by a Japanese paraphrase about deep feeling. The printed canǒ. i, sequence is separated correctly, not fused into a word.
The Japanese paraphrase concerns heartfelt joy. The reading ſomite is retained, and the Portuguese co- continues as ração on the next line.
Ração completes coração, giving the sense of rejoicing from the heart. It is an indented continuation of the Tanpu example.
Tanquano cuchibiru describes red and attractive lips. The source's Peiços is retained, with the comparison to a named flower continuing below.
The lips are compared to a flower called Botan. Botan is a whole Japanese term embedded in Portuguese explanation and is recorded in typeface_terms, unlike an ordinary headword.

runs.text: Certa feição de candieiro de Iapão.

lines.note: Tanqei denotes a particular form of Japanese lamp. The source gives no further construction details on this complete single-line entry.
Tanqi, glossed by Mijicai qi, means anger or irritation. Its examples continue at the top of the next column and must stay connected to this headword.
The first example means becoming angry. A pilcrow introduces a second example divided Tã- / qiuo across lines, continuing the Tanqi entry from the left column.
The opening fragment completes Tãqiuo in an expression for calming anger. This closes the examples under Tanqi.
Tãqina mono describes an irritable or frenzied person. The nasal abbreviations and the absence of visible terminal punctuation are retained.
Tanren concerns practice or training, with Neri, ru as its Japanese gloss. The Portuguese explanation continues with something already learned.

runs.text: eſtà aprendido pera mais ſe perfeiçcar, ou habi-

lines.note: Practice improves what one has learned. The apparent c after ç in perfeiçcar is retained; a damaged o cannot be excluded, so the anomaly is documented rather than silently normalized.

runs.text: to, & experiencia do que hum tem aprẽdido, &

lines.note: The line completes habito and describes acquired habit and experience in what one has learned. It continues the same definition rather than starting a new sense label.
The explanation ends with what has been practised, followed by Tanrenſuru as the verbal example. The close-set Japanese compound is retained as printed.
Unaccented Tanrio means anger or irritation. It is distinct from the later Tanriǒ with a marked final vowel, which denotes a sweet drink.
Tanriona fito describes an angry or irritable person. This is a separate complete entry derived from the anger-related Tanrio.
Tanriojin is equated with Tanrio mono, an irritable or choleric person. The second Portuguese equivalent continues on the next line.
Colerico completes the description of an angry or hot-tempered person. It closes Tanriojin and should not be joined to the following drink-related entry.
Tanriǒ, glossed by Amazaqe, is described as sweet wine. Its marked final vowel distinguishes it from the preceding anger-related Tanrio entries.
Tanſai denotes slight or weak learning. Vſui chye is retained because no secure i is visible between h and y; the worn spelling is documented without supplying a letter.
Ber completes the divided Portuguese saber. The historical comparison describes an unlearned person, followed by Xenchi tanſai as a synonymous expression.
Idem refers back to little learning; no extra pilcrow precedes it. A new example describes an unlearned person, with Ho- continuing as mem below.
The fragment completes Homem idiota, here the source's description of an unlearned person. The historical wording is preserved without imposing a modern clinical interpretation.

runs.text: Certa caixinha como eſcritorio em que

lines.note: Tanſu is a small chest compared with a writing cabinet. The next line specifies the tea-related implements it contains.
The chest holds implements for Chanoyu. The embedded Japanese term is visibly italic within the Portuguese explanation and is flagged in typeface_terms without silently making it roman.
Tanſui is defined as phlegm. This short complete entry retains the historical Portuguese form Freimas and is separate from the adverbial headword below.
Tantanto is labelled an adverb describing overflowing. Vt announces the Japanese examples on the next physical line.

runs.text: Tantanto xite aru. l, tatayete aru.

lines.note: Two alternative expressions illustrate the overflowing sense. Their common Portuguese translation begins Eſtar and continues below.
Tresbordando completes the translation as being in an overflowing state. It closes the examples under Tantanto.
Tanteqi means immediately, at that very instant. The compact definition is complete on this physical line.
This Tanto refers by Idem to the immediately preceding sense, at once. It must remain distinct from the following homograph meaning much in quantity.
This separate Tanto is labelled an adverb meaning much in quantity. It does not inherit the temporal meaning of the preceding homograph.
Tanuqi names an animal compared with an adibe. The comparison word reads adibe, not acibe; the transcription does not replace the historical comparison with a modern species gloss.
Tanxa, also tanja, names the red medicinal substance encountered on the preceding page. The adjective is divided ver- / melha across the physical lines.

runs.text: melha, que tambem ſerue de tinta vermelha.

lines.note: The substance is red and also serves as red pigment. This is a historical description of its uses, not a modern medical recommendation.

runs.text: Poſto q̃ na pratica ſe diz ordinariamẽte,

lines.note: The source says that ordinary usage calls the substance Tan. The readings ordinariamẽte and Tan are incorporated despite worn medial letters and final n; Tan is flagged as embedded Japanese.
This distinct Tanxa means a small amount, glossed by Mijicaqu and ſucoxi. It is not merged with the red-substance homograph above.
Tanxeqi is glossed by Aſayǔ, morning and evening. The nasal mark is placed on the second a in Menhaã; its abraded shape remains nonblocking uncertainty, while terminal S. is roman.
Tanxǒ means a short letter, with a Japanese paraphrase. The marked final vowel is retained instead of assimilating this form to the next unmarked headword.
Tanxo is another expression for a short letter, referring back by Idem. Its unmarked final o is preserved as printed.
Tanya denotes a short night, glossed by Mijicaqi yo. The Portuguese pe- continues as quena on the next line.
Quena completes pequena, an alternative description of the short night. This is an indented continuation of Tanya, not a separate entry.
Tanyacu is equated with Neriguſuri, a prepared medicinal compound. The description of its composition continues on the following line.
The preparation is composed from several ingredients or preparations. The historical medicinal description is retained without adding a recipe or recommending its use.
Tanye is glossed as a short garment. The adjective curto is divided at the physical line boundary, and the usage label appears below.
To completes curto. The terminal S. is a roman usage label outside the italic Portuguese definition, and the line closes Tanye.
Tanzocu means searching anxiously and with great diligence. The divided di- continues as ligencia on the next line.
The definition adds care and introduces Tãzocu ſuru as the verb phrase. Its nasal abbreviation is retained rather than expanded to match the headword spelling.
Tappai, glossed by Cotaye vogamu, concerns warm reception and respect. The Portuguese agaſalha- continues below.
The welcome-and-respect definition ends, followed by an example beginning Chiſô tappaiuo tçu-. Its verb continues on the next physical line.
Cuſu completes tçucuſu. The example means giving a very warm welcome and showing affection and respect; moſ- continues below.
This completes mostrar and the example's expression of much affection and respect. It closes the Tappai entry.
Tappit denotes an accomplished writer or calligrapher, glossed by Taxxita fide. The double x and the reading eſcriuão, not eſcritão, are retained.

These adjectival and attributive person forms repeat the accomplished-writer sense. The nasals in Tappinna and tappinno are worn; the incorporated readings are supported by the constructions and remain documented uncertainties.
